messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mahmoud, a 54-year-old Middle Eastern man and software engineer, has been grappling with severe distress following a traumatic sexual assault that occurred over two years ago. The event was deeply scarring for him, leaving lasting psychological wounds that have shaped his daily life ever since. The incident itself happened in an isolated alley near Mahmoud’s apartment building late one evening. He had just finished working overtime and was on his way home when he encountered a man who aggressively forced him into the dark alleyway. The assailant was wearing military-style clothing, which now serves as a potent trigger for Mahmoud. Even the sound of sirens or seeing an ambulance can evoke vivid memories of that night, bringing back overwhelming feelings of fear and helplessness. Mahmoud’s triggers have led to several maladaptive strategies in his daily life. He avoids going near his apartment building after dark and has developed an aversion to military uniforms and weapons, which he associates with the attacker. This avoidance extends to authority figures and anyone wearing a uniform. For example, he recently avoided taking public transportation because of the presence of police officers at the station, even though it meant a much longer walk home. The constant fear that something dangerous might happen again has driven Mahmoud to rely heavily on maladaptive strategies for safety. He now only feels secure in his small circle of familiar places — primarily his apartment and certain stores he knows well. This limited safe zone has become increasingly restrictive as his fears have grown over time. What frightened him most was the realization that even his own home didn’t feel entirely safe anymore. Mahmoud’s negative appraisals have compounded these issues, making it harder for him to cope with everyday situations. He feels deeply unjustified by what happened to him and harbors a strong sense of self-blame, believing that if he had acted differently, the assault might not have occurred. These beliefs exacerbate his avoidance behaviors, as he perceives any unfamiliar environment or person in authority as a potential threat. The cycle has become increasingly vicious over time. Mahmoud’s constant scanning for danger and experiencing false alarms have led to heightened anxiety, which further reinforces his maladaptive strategies. The more he avoids certain places and situations, the more convinced he becomes that they are inherently dangerous. This pattern of avoidance and threat monitoring has significantly impacted his work as a software engineer, where he often finds himself reluctant to attend meetings or work in environments with authority figures present. These behaviors have also strained Mahmoud’s relationships. He feels isolated and disconnected from others because he is always on high alert, avoiding social interactions that might trigger memories of the assault. His self-blame has intensified over time, leading him to feel that he deserves this pain, which only deepens his isolation and fear. What finally brought Mahmoud to seek help was a recent incident where sirens blared near his home, triggering intense panic and causing him to flee from his apartment into the night. This event highlighted how far his condition had progressed, leaving him feeling vulnerable and overwhelmed. Despite his fears, he hopes that therapy can provide some relief and allow him to regain control over his life. Mahmoud is most afraid of never being able to feel safe again or return to a normal emotional state. However, he also holds onto the hope that with proper support, he might be able to break the cycle of avoidance and find ways to manage his fears more effectively.
